newsitem.title: UK: EU sugar exports seen pressured by central America.
newsitem.headline: EU sugar exports seen pressured by central America.

text.p: European Union (EU) sugar exporters are being squeezed in some traditional markets by alternative suppliers such as Mexico which can produce a range of different qualities, brokers said on Thursday.
Mexican 45 ICUMSA sugars could be bought and shipped to west Africa at roughly the same cost as the same-quality EU equivalent, they said.
"At the moment the 45 ICUMSA is the same price from the EU as it is from anywhere else," said one trader.

"The discount you get for the Mexican 45s and the additional freight equals the same as the stuff you get for EUs," she said, but noted that the shipment would have to come from a Gulf port such as Veracruz.
Traders quoted a premium of between $3 and $4 over London's spot May futures contract for EU cargoes.
One broker suggested that even with the premium at a relatively low level, the market expected that it would move even lower and so some buyers in west Africa were holding back.
"We seem to have got this impasse where prices are a little above what people want to pay and the bids below. I'm not sure a great deal is trading."
Even though Europe as a whole is generally thought to have failed to set a production record from this year's beet crops, the outturn was still above expectations.
The main reason for the dominance of Mexico as a quality supplier in the western hemisphere is the absence of Brazil as an exporter before its new crop starts in a few months' time.

Buyers expecting to take delivery of sugar which they had earlier contracted to import from Brazil were taking up offers from central American producers because Brazilian cargoes had dried up, traders said.
In its latest report, Czarnikow Sugar said some millers had bought back cargoes to satisfy a strong domestic market, thus reducing the already minimal supply of Brazilian whites.
New crop Brazilian cargoes of 45 ICUMSA sugar were recently quoted at a $10 discount to May for June/July.
Most countries in west Africa tended to take smaller deliveries and were importing both Mexican and EU sugars whereas they normally took Brazilian cargoes.
"Mexicans have taken the place of some of the Brazilian sales and they have been very good quality," the broker said.

"Some of that (African requirement) is being filled either from Europe in smaller vessels dropping off a couple of thousand tonnes to each (country) and some is coming straight across, filling earlier contracts."

On Wednesday, for example, shipbrokers said E D & F Man fixed 9/11,000 tonnes in bags from Eemshaven to Lagos for mid-March and quoted for a further 14,000 tonnes from Veracruz or Coatzacoalcos to Algeria for prompt dates.

Guatemala, another key central American exporter, is also producing 45 ICUMSA sugars and qualities as low as 220 ICUMSA. But the low-quality Guatemalan cargoes are scarce, even though demand for them has been seen in east Africa, traders said.

"There are markets within the western hemisphere for those lower qualities but obviously the majority of the countries there are primarily exporters. The obvious candidate is Venezuela," said one analyst.
Traders said the few top-quality cargoes tended to be traded around the Caribbean and west coast of South America and were unlikely to be shipped towards Europe.
